cues.text: A jam to clear, a line to break, a vessel to open.
You know these jobs. But today, something might be different.
So before your hands move, give it two minutes. That's the 2-minute rule.
It's a short pause you take on purpose, at the point of work, where you do the job.
Do it before you start, and again after any break, handover, interruption or change.
Two minutes is a guide, not an exact time. What matters is the pause.
You already do line clearance for product, right before each run.
The 2-minute rule is line clearance for people.
It adds to your procedures, permits and lockout. It never replaces them.
But you're the one at the job, so you can see what the plan missed.
Here's how. Stop: hands off.
Look: around the job, and compare it with the plan.
Ask yourself four questions: What's different? What could hurt us?
Checked or assumed? What if it goes wrong?
“Checked or assumed” means: did you look or test it yourself, or are you guessing?
Then decide: make one of three calls. Go, Fix it, or Stop & get help.
Fix it only if you're trained and authorized, and it's a step in your procedure.
No permit yet? Someone else's unfinished work? Not authorized? Stop & get help.
Not sure, or the fix doesn't work? Stop & get help.
Let's try it on a routine job: you're about to clean a weighing booth.
What's different? Nothing. What could hurt us? Leftover powder and the cleaning chemical.
Gloves and goggles are on. Checked or assumed? Checked: the airflow light is green.
What if it goes wrong? The spill kit is right there. Your call?
Go. That took just a few seconds.
Most pauses end like that.
But sometimes a question catches a problem. That's a save. Here are six.
They're examples built from common pharma hazards, not real events.
In each save, the video asks you twice: find the problem, then pick your call.
Save one: you take over a tablet press at handover.
What would make you stop here?
What's different? The handover note says the last shift started a tooling change.
The guard is open, the tooling is half in, and there's no lock on the power switch.
Your call?
Stop & get help. It's someone else's unfinished work.
Your lead comes over, thanks you, and checks with the last shift.
An authorized press setter locks out, tries START, then finishes and counts the tooling.
Guard closed, area clear, setter's lock removed, interlock tested. Then Go.
Nobody starts that press with its tooling half in.
Save two: you add powder from a drum to a reactor that holds flammable solvent.
It's inerted: filled with nitrogen to keep the oxygen out.
Before you start, what would make you stop here?
What could hurt us? A static spark at the open manway, where there's solvent vapor.
Checked or assumed? The oxygen is below the limit, but the grounding indicator is red.
What's your call?
Fix it. It's a step in your procedure: clip the grounding clamp onto the drum.
The indicator turns green, and the drum liner is static-safe. Now it's Go.
The spark never happens.
Save three: a product change. As a contractor, you'll open a filter dryer full of nitrogen.
So, what would make you stop here?
What could hurt us? Low-oxygen air inside. You can't see it or smell it.
Checked or assumed? Is the nitrogen line closed with a solid plate, and the air inside tested?
Not yet, and no permit yet.
Your call?
Stop & get help: opening it needs a gas test and a permit.
An authorized team isolates, tests, ventilates and retests. Once the permit is issued, it's Go.
No permit, no Go.
Nobody leans into air with too little oxygen.
Save four: an interruption. The blister packer jams where your jam tool can't reach.
It's stopped, but stopped isn't the same as isolated.
So you lock out power and air.
Now, what would make you stop here?
Checked or assumed? The gauge still shows trapped air.
What's your call?
Fix it. Your procedure lets you bleed off the trapped air, with your own lock still on.
Bleed to zero and try START. Nothing moves, so it's Go.
Your hand never goes into a machine that still has stored energy.
Save five: after a break, you weigh a potent active ingredient at an isolator.
Look closely. What would make you stop here?
What's different? Nothing, and the pressure display is in range.
Checked or assumed? You check each glove, and one has a cut.
Your call?
Stop & get help, because a cut glove is a break in the barrier. Your lead and QA must know.
An authorized person changes the glove and leak-tests it. Then Go.
That powder is strong, even in tiny amounts. It stays inside the isolator.
Save six: you have a permit to open a pipe at the transfer panel. That's a line break.
The CIP screen says the cleaning cycle is complete.
Your turn. What would make you stop here?
What if it goes wrong? If the pipe still has pressure, where would it spray?
You lock out the supply valve and the pump, step to the side, and check the gauge.
It shows pressure, and the line is hot.
So, what's your call?
Fix it. Your line-break procedure says: wait, vent, check for zero pressure and a cool line.
Then Go. The screen reports the cycle. The gauge reports your line.
No one gets sprayed with hot cleaning chemical or steam.
Three saves were Fix it, and three were Stop & get help. All six end in Go, once it's safe.
And most pauses end in Go right away. That's good for people, product and the line.
Anyone can stop a job, staff or contractor, even on a late batch. No punishment, no blame.
When you stop, leaders come quickly and thank you, fix the cause and tell you what changed.
The pause isn't a form. Just report what you caught the usual way.
So, before you start, and after any break, handover, interruption or change: stop and look.
Ask: What's different? What could hurt us?
Checked or assumed? What if it goes wrong?
Decide: Go, Fix it, or Stop & get help.
Fix it only if you're trained and authorized, and it's a step in your procedure.
When in doubt, get help. That's the 2-minute rule: line clearance for people.
Find out who to call for help: days, nights and weekends.
Follow your site's procedures. This video is awareness training only.
